concept.name: Adaptive Radix Trees (ART): Path Compression, SIMD Node Layouts & Optimistic Lock Coupling
concept.title: Adaptive Radix Trees (ART): Path Compression, SIMD Node Layouts & Optimistic Lock Coupling
concept.tagline: O(k) byte-keyed lookups with four adaptive node sizes (Node4/16/48/256) and zero pointer-chasing locks.
concept.purpose: Understand why classic 256-way radix tries waste gigabytes of RAM, why B+Trees stall on key comparisons at every level, and how ART achieves both compact memory and cache-friendly SIMD lookups.

prerequisites.title: Tries & Radix Trees
prerequisites.summary: Know how prefix trees branch on key bytes instead of comparing whole keys, giving O(k) lookup time independent of dataset size N.

prerequisites.title: CPU Cache Lines & SIMD
prerequisites.summary: Understand that a single 64-byte cache line miss costs ~60–100 ns, while SSE2/AVX2 can compare 16 bytes in a single CPU instruction.

spark.summary: Adaptive Radix Trees shrink trie memory by 10x+ using four dynamically sized node layouts (Node4, Node16, Node48, Node256) plus path compression, and scale to 64+ cores via Optimistic Lock Coupling.
spark.keyTakeaway: When an in-memory ordered index is bottlenecked by B+Tree key-comparison cache misses or 256-way trie memory bloat, use an Adaptive Radix Tree with Node4/16/48/256 layouts and path compression so lookup cost scales with key length k instead of log N.
spark.byteSummary:
A standard 256-way radix trie gives O(k) lookup time for k-byte keys without balancing, but every inner node allocates 256 child pointers (2 KB per node) even when only 2 or 3 children exist—wasting over 95% of RAM on sparse keys. Conversely, an in-memory B+Tree packs memory tightly but performs binary search over full keys at every tree level, triggering expensive cache misses and branch mispredictions.

The Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), introduced by Leis et al. for HyPer, solves both problems by adapting each inner node's physical layout to its actual fanout: Node4 stores up to 4 sorted keys + pointers (48 bytes); Node16 stores up to 16 keys and compares all 16 in one SSE2/SIMD instruction; Node48 uses a 256-byte index array pointing into 48 child slots; and Node256 uses a direct 256-entry pointer table for dense branches. Lazy Expansion and Path Compression collapse single-child chains into a compact prefix header, capping tree height at the number of distinct keys.

To scale ART across dozens of CPU cores without reader-writer lock contention, Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC) replaces lock acquisition on reads with a per-node 64-bit version word: readers check the version before and after reading a node and simply restart if a writer mutated it, keeping read paths 100% write-free in shared L1/L2 caches.

learningJourney.title: P · Problem & Why Classic Tries and B+Trees Stall
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Exposes the memory-vs-cache-miss dilemma in in-memory ordered indexes.

explanation.foundation: If you index 100 million 64-bit integers in a standard 256-way radix trie (8 levels, 1 byte per level), every sparse inner node allocates 256 * 8-byte pointers = 2,048 bytes just to store 2 or 3 children.
explanation.core: That wastes >90% of DRAM on null pointers. On the other hand, a B+Tree has depth log_B(N) (~4–5 levels for 100M keys), but at every level it binary-searches 64–256 keys, causing unpredictable branch mispredictions and repeated full-key comparisons (especially costly for variable-length strings).
explanation.deepDive: A hash table gives O(1) point lookups but cannot serve range scans (`BETWEEN`, prefix `LIKE 'app%'`, or `ORDER BY`). ART preserves lexicographical order for range queries while keeping inner-node memory under ~52 bytes/key on average.

learningJourney.title: R · Representation: Node4, Node16, Node48 & Node256
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Shows how four physical node layouts trade off memory compactness and lookup speed.

explanation.foundation: Instead of one giant node struct, ART uses four node sizes and promotes/demotes a node as children are inserted or deleted.
explanation.core: Node4 (<=4 children) fits in a single 64-byte cache line using sorted key bytes. Node16 (5–16 children) stores up to 16 key bytes and uses `_mm_cmpeq_epi8` + `_mm_movemask_epi8` to test all 16 bytes in parallel. Node48 (17–48 children) uses a 256-byte lookup array mapping byte -> slot index [0..47], avoiding 256 * 8B = 2 KB pointers. Node256 (49–256 children) uses a direct `children[byte]` array for O(1) indexing.
explanation.deepDive: Memory footprint comparison for 48 children: Node256 takes 2,048 bytes of pointers, whereas Node48 takes 256 bytes (index) + 48 * 8 bytes (pointers) = 640 bytes—a 3.2x reduction while staying O(1)!

learningJourney.title: I · Invariant: Lazy Expansion & Path Compression
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Prevents 1-child chains from blowing up memory and pointer-chasing latency on long keys.

explanation.foundation: Suppose two keys are `/api/v1/users/1001` and `/api/v1/users/1002`. A naive trie creates 14 single-child inner nodes just for `/api/v1/users/100`.
explanation.core: ART eliminates those nodes with two rules: (1) Lazy Expansion—never create inner nodes for a single leaf; store the full suffix in the leaf until a second key shares a prefix. (2) Path Compression—store the common prefix bytes directly in the inner node header so lookup skips all shared bytes in one `memcmp`.
explanation.deepDive: To bound inner node header size, ART stores up to 8–10 prefix bytes inline (`prefix[0..7]` + `prefix_len`). If `prefix_len > 8`, optimistic path compression skips comparing the remaining bytes during traversal and verifies the full key once at the leaf.

learningJourney.title: M · Mechanics at Scale: Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC)
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Eliminates reader cache-line ping-pong across 64+ CPU cores.

explanation.foundation: Even a shared reader-writer lock (`pthread_rwlock`) writes a reader count to memory on every read, causing CPU cache-line bouncing across cores.
explanation.core: With Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC), each ART node carries an atomic 64-bit `version_lock_obsolete` word: bit 0 is the write lock, bit 1 marks an obsolete/replaced node, and the upper bits are a monotonic version counter. Readers never write to memory—they load `v = node.read_lock_or_restart()`, read child pointers, and call `node.read_unlock_or_restart(v)`. If `v` changed or bit 0/1 was set, the reader simply restarts from the root.
explanation.deepDive: Writers acquire the parent's write lock and child's write lock (lock coupling), bump the version counter on unlock, and when growing a Node4 -> Node16, mark the old Node4 obsolete and hand it to Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) so concurrent optimistic readers never dereference freed memory.

decisionFramework.problem: How to scale an ordered in-memory index across 64+ CPU cores with minimal read contention.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a global RWLock or per-node RWLock on every traversal.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Every reader mutates the lock's atomic counter, invalidating the cache line across all other cores.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Per-node RWLocks vs. Lock-Free Bw-Tree vs. ART + Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC).
decisionFramework.decision: Use ART with OLC: version-validated lock-free reads + fine-grained per-node write locks + Epoch-Based Reclamation.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Readers never dirty cache lines, at the cost of occasional read restarts under heavy write contention on the same node.

learningJourney.title: E · Edge Cases, Assumptions & When NOT to Use ART
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Clarifies key-encoding traps, null-byte termination, and when hash tables or B+Trees win.

explanation.foundation: ART compares raw unsigned bytes from left to right. If you insert signed integers (`-5` vs `+5`) or variable-length strings where one key is a prefix of another (`'app'` and `'apple'`), naive byte ordering breaks!
explanation.core: Fix both deterministically: (1) Flip the sign bit on signed integers and store in big-endian byte order so unsigned byte order matches numeric order; (2) Append a `0x00` sentinel byte to variable-length strings (or store leaf pointers with key-length metadata) so no key is a prefix of another.
explanation.deepDive: When NOT to use ART: if your dataset is larger than RAM and lives on NVMe/SSD pages, a disk-paged B+Tree or LSM-Tree beats ART because 4 KB/16 KB page I/O dominates; if you only ever need exact-match lookups (`GET key`) with zero range scans, an open-addressed hash table (SwissTable) is simpler and faster. Glossary: ART (Adaptive Radix Tree), OLC (Optimistic Lock Coupling), EBR (Epoch-Based Reclamation), SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data).

decisionExercise.prompt: You are indexing 50M variable-length UTF-8 strings (`'user'`, `'user_123'`, `'user_123_pro'`) in an in-memory ART. Lookups for `'user'` fail or collide with `'user_123'`. What invariant was violated?

options.label: Node256 was used instead of Node4.
options.explanation: Node size only affects physical storage, not prefix termination.

options.label: Keys were not prefix-free: `'user'` is a prefix of `'user_123'`, so keys must be null-terminated (`0x00`) or inner nodes must hold an optional leaf pointer.
options.explanation: Correct! In a radix tree, if one key is a prefix of another, you must append a sentinel byte (for C-strings without embedded nulls) or allow inner nodes to reference a prefix-ending leaf.

options.label: Optimistic Lock Coupling requires keys to be 8 bytes.
options.explanation: OLC works for arbitrary key lengths.

steps.title: Optimistic Prefix Skip & Read
steps.explanation: Reader loads even version 12 without writing any lock word, skips the compressed prefix, and reads the child pointer.

steps.title: 5th Child Triggers Node4 -> Node16
steps.explanation: Writer locks Node4, allocates a 16-slot SIMD Node16, swaps the parent pointer, and marks the old Node4 obsolete.

steps.title: Concurrent Reader Detects Skew
steps.explanation: Reader sees version changed from 12 to 13 (obsolete bit set) and cleanly restarts from the root without corruption.

steps.title: Epoch Advances & Frees Old Node4
steps.explanation: Once all active reader epochs pass e+1, EBR safely frees the retired Node4.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does ART's Node48 use a 256-byte index array plus 48 child pointers instead of 256 direct pointers?

options.text: It cuts node pointer memory from 2,048 bytes down to 640 bytes while keeping O(1) byte-indexed child lookup.
options.feedback: Correct! 256 * 1B index + 48 * 8B pointers = 640 bytes vs. 2,048 bytes for Node256.

options.text: Because CPUs cannot allocate arrays of 256 pointers.
options.feedback: Node256 uses 256 pointers directly when fanout exceeds 48.

options.text: To force binary search over 48 keys.
options.feedback: Node48 does O(1) direct indexing into the 256-byte array, not binary search.

options.text: To eliminate the need for path compression.
options.feedback: Path compression is orthogonal to node fanout sizing.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Node48 bridges the gap between SIMD-scanned Node16 and 2 KB Node256 with O(1) lookup at ~3x less RAM.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens in Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC) if a writer modifies an ART node while a reader is traversing it?

options.text: The reader blocks on a mutex until the writer finishes.
options.feedback: OLC readers never acquire locks or block.

options.text: The reader detects the version counter change (or obsolete bit) during validation and restarts its traversal.
options.feedback: Correct! Version validation turns concurrent structural changes into cheap read retries.

options.text: The reader silently returns partial data from the old node.
The writer aborts its own update to let readers proceed.
options.feedback: Writers hold exclusive node locks and always complete.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: OLC keeps read paths 100% write-free in L1/L2 cache by validating monotonic node versions.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must signed 64-bit integers have their sign bit flipped and be stored in big-endian byte order before insertion into ART?

options.text: So unsigned byte-by-byte radix order matches signed numeric order (`-10 < -1 < 0 < 5`).
options.feedback: Correct! Big-endian puts the most significant byte first, and flipping the sign bit maps `INT64_MIN` to `0x00...` and `INT64_MAX` to `0xFF...`.

options.text: Because x86 CPUs only support big-endian arithmetic.
options.feedback: x86 is little-endian; that's exactly why byte-swapping is required.

options.text: To make Node16 SIMD instructions work on 64-bit pointers.
options.feedback: Node16 compares 1-byte key slices, not 64-bit pointers.

options.text: To prevent Epoch-Based Reclamation from freeing integers.
options.feedback: EBR manages node memory, not key byte ordering.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Order-preserving key encoding is mandatory for radix range scans (`BETWEEN`, `<`, `>`) to return keys in true numeric order.

beginner.summary: Adaptive Radix Trees shrink prefix-tree memory by resizing each node (4, 16, 48, or 256 slots) to match how many children it actually has.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When a plain radix tree wastes too much RAM on sparse keys, resize nodes dynamically between 4 and 256 slots and collapse single-child paths.
beginner.byteSummary: Instead of giving every tree node 256 slots, ART starts small with 4 slots and grows to 16, 48, or 256 only when needed. Combined with path compression, it gives fast O(k) lookups without wasting memory.

intermediate.summary: ART pairs four adaptive node layouts (Node4/16/48/256) with path compression and Optimistic Lock Coupling for fast ordered in-memory indexing.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When an in-memory ordered index stalls on B+Tree comparison misses, use ART with SIMD Node16 scans and OLC version validation.
intermediate.byteSummary: ART adapts fanout across Node4, SIMD Node16, indexed Node48, and direct Node256 while collapsing single-child chains. OLC lets readers traverse without dirtying cache lines.

advanced.summary: Cache-conscious ART with optimistic path compression, big-endian sign-flipped keys, OLC version validation, and EBR safe node reclamation.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When scaling an in-memory OLTP index across 64+ cores, pair ART + OLC with Epoch-Based Reclamation and order-preserving key encoding.
advanced.byteSummary: By combining 16-byte SIMD comparisons, optimistic prefix skipping, write-free OLC version validation, and Epoch-Based Reclamation for Node4->16->48->256 transitions, ART sustains tens of millions of concurrent ops/sec.
